## Defects in the memo's reasoning

### 1. Webinar attendance → retention

**a. Survivorship bias in the sample itself.**
The analysis is restricted to the 412 customers *still active on Pro today*. Customers who already churned — whether or not they attended a webinar — are excluded entirely before the comparison is made. This means the "31% higher retention" figure is computed only among survivors, which is close to meaningless as a measure of what drove retention: you cannot learn what predicts churn by looking exclusively at people who didn't churn. This would cause the effect size to be biased in an unknown direction and unable to support any causal or even predictive claim about attendance and churn.

**b. Likely immortal-time bias.**
Related to (a): webinar attendance is something that happens (or doesn't) shortly after signup. A customer who churns very early has little or no chance to "attend a webinar" before leaving, so early churners get disproportionately counted in the non-attendee group. This mechanically inflates the attendee group's apparent retention advantage, independent of any real effect of webinars. This would cause the 31% gap to overstate any genuine effect, possibly entirely explaining it.

**c. Correlation treated as causation.**
Even setting aside (a)/(b), customers who voluntarily attend an onboarding webinar are self-selected: they are plausibly more engaged, more motivated to succeed with the product, or simply more organized — traits independently associated with staying subscribed. The memo asserts "webinars therefore cause higher retention" with no control for this confound (no randomization, no matching, no adjustment for baseline engagement). This would cause the company to misattribute an engagement effect to the webinar itself.

**d. Extrapolating from voluntary attendees to a mandatory policy.**
Even if the correlation were causal for the kind of customer who currently opts in, that doesn't imply the same effect holds when attendance is *compelled* for everyone. Forcing disengaged customers into a webinar changes the composition and nature of "attendance" (compliance vs. genuine interest), so the observed lift may not transfer. This would cause the mandatory-attendance policy to underdeliver relative to the projected 31% benefit, or fail to move retention at all.

### 2. Central region churn → spend recommendation

**a. Multiple-comparisons problem (data dredging).**
Eighteen attributes were tested against churn, and one came back at p = 0.04. With 18 independent tests at α = 0.05, the probability of finding at least one "significant" result purely by chance is roughly 1 − 0.95¹⁸ ≈ 60%. A single p = 0.04 result out of 18 tests is exactly the kind of finding you'd expect from noise alone, and it does not survive standard corrections (e.g., Bonferroni would require p < 0.05/18 ≈ 0.0028). This would cause the company to chase a false positive — reallocating budget toward a region that has no real churn advantage.

**b. Marginal significance treated as strong evidence.**
Independent of the multiple-testing issue, p = 0.04 is only barely under the conventional 0.05 threshold — weak evidence on its own for a resource-allocation decision, and weaker still once the search over 18 attributes is accounted for.

**c. No causal mechanism identified.**
Even if the regional effect were real, "Central region churns less" is descriptive, not explanatory — nothing in the memo identifies *why* (demographics, industry mix, pricing, account age, etc.). Concentrating spend there assumes spend can influence or leverage whatever is producing the effect, which hasn't been established. This would cause spend to be misdirected if the underlying driver is unrelated to anything more investment can affect (e.g., regional customers happen to be a different company-size mix).

### 3. Satisfaction increase → support model

**a. Correlation-causation fallacy with no ruled-out alternatives.**
The memo attributes the 62%→66% change entirely to "the new support model" without considering other explanations occurring in the same quarter: seasonality, product changes, pricing changes, changes in the survey population/response rate, or simple regression to the mean. No control group or before/after design isolates the support model as the cause. This would cause the company to credit (and keep investing in) a program that may have had little or nothing to do with the observed change.

**b. No test of statistical significance.**
Unlike the churn analysis (which at least reports a p-value), the satisfaction change is given no significance test, confidence interval, or sample size. A 4-point move could easily be within normal quarter-to-quarter sampling noise. This would cause a possibly-random fluctuation to be read as a confirmed program effect.

### What is *not* a defect (for completeness)
The arithmetic in each section is internally consistent, and I'm not flagging the numbers themselves (as instructed). I'd also note the "4% improvement" phrasing conflates percentage points (a 4-point rise) with a percent change (~6.5% relative) — this doesn't affect the causal conclusion but is worth tightening since it sits next to two other statistics (31%, p=0.04) that are easy to conflate with it.
